title: How do you talk about risks in a case without sounding vague?
description: Risk checklist for case interviews. When you are asked "What are the risks?" or need to close a recommendation.
hook: Talk about risks by naming two or three specific ones, grouped as business, operations, strategy or regulation, putting a rough size on the biggest, and pairing each with a way to reduce it. "There are some risks" earns nothing; "a three-month construction delay would cost about $900,000, so we should pilot two stores first" earns a lot.
body:
When it helps

Use this when the interviewer asks "What are the risks?" and at the end of every recommendation, where one or two risks and next steps should follow your answer. It also helps in market entry and investment cases, where risks decide whether a good-looking plan is worth doing.

The checklist

Business

  • Demand lower than planned
  • Competitors react
  • Prices fall

Operations

  • Delays and cost overruns
  • Quality or supply problems
  • Skills the client lacks

Strategy

  • Distracts from the core business
  • Hurts the brand
  • Locks the client in

Regulation and economy

  • Laws and approvals
  • Politics
  • Exchange rates and the economy

An example: a coffee chain enters Germany

You recommend that a UK coffee chain opens in Germany. Business: German customers may not take to the brand, and local chains may cut prices. Operations: finding sites and staff may take longer than planned. Strategy: management attention is pulled from the home market. Regulation and economy: different employment rules and the euro exchange rate. Then pick the two that matter most and say how to reduce each.

Put a number on the biggest risk

Suppose the recommendation is to open ten new stores, which together will earn an illustrative $300,000 a month in contribution once open. "Execution risk" tells the client nothing. This does:

"If construction overruns by three months, we lose 3 × $300,000 = $900,000 of contribution, before any extra rent while the stores sit empty."

For each important risk, give four things: the trigger, the size of the downside, the likelihood if you can estimate it sensibly, and the mitigation. If you think the delay has a 30% chance, the expected cost is 30% × $900,000 = $270,000, which tells the client how much it is worth spending to avoid it.

Match each risk to a fix:

  • Weak demand: open two pilot stores and expand only if sales per store hit an agreed level.
  • Supplier delays: secure a second supplier before rollout.
  • Uncertain regulation: get legal advice before signing anything irreversible.

How it sounds in an interview

"The main risks are that demand is lower than we expect and that rivals cut prices. To reduce them, I'd start with a pilot in one city and agree clear targets before expanding."

The weak version lists eight risks in one breath, from "the economy" to "competition", with no size, no priority and no fix.

Common mistakes

  • Naming categories ("market risk") instead of specific events.
  • Giving every risk equal time. Focus on those that could change the recommendation, especially irreversible spending, reliance on one customer or supplier, and safety or legal limits.
  • Raising a risk with no way to reduce or monitor it.

Practise it

1. You recommend a manufacturer builds a $50M plant. Give two specific risks with mitigations.

Show the answer

Demand: if orders come in 20% below plan, the plant runs half-empty for years; mitigate by signing supply contracts with key customers before committing. Construction: overruns could add cost and delay; mitigate with a fixed-price contract and a buffer in the budget. Then say what you would monitor: orders signed and construction milestones.

2. A delay would cost $2M and has a 25% chance. A step that removes the risk costs $300,000. Is it worth it?

Show the answer

Expected cost of the delay: 25% × $2M = $500,000, more than the $300,000 cost of avoiding it, so yes on expected value. It is even more attractive if a $2M hit would cause serious problems for the client.

Where to practise next

Practise closing a case in the 60-second recommendation, then try Desert Dairy (should a dairy company build a new plant?).
